name: Hive (Yianni, 2001) - core ruleset
one_line: Randomness-free abstract tile-laying game about surrounding the opponent's queen using bug-specific movement constraints, no board.
take_what: the One Hive rule: no move may ever split the connected mass of tiles into two groups, and no placed piece may ever be isolated - every single placement/move is filtered through this global connectivity check
constraint: none - public domain mechanic, not IP-protected rule text

name: BoardGameArena Hive rules doc
one_line: Canonical digital-implementation rules reference for Hive including sliding and freedom-to-move constraints.
take_what: the 'Freedom to Move' / sliding rule: a piece can only physically slide from one adjacent hex to another if the gap it slides through is wide enough (not pinched between two occupied hexes on both sides) - movement is blocked by geometry, not just occupancy

name: Play Hive Like a Champion (2nd ed.) - strategy book TOC
one_line: Full strategy-book table of contents naming Hive's formal tactical vocabulary: Pin, Cover, Block, Fill, Shutout, Squeeze, Two Beetle Attack.
take_what: named, teachable tactical patterns with fixed board shapes (Gate, Door, Ring, Elbow, Pocket) that recur across games - the design deliberately names recurring geometric formations so players build pattern-recognition vocabulary, the same way chess names forks/pins/forks
constraint: none - concept, not text to copy

name: Hive Board Game Strategy Guide - The Gamers Guides
one_line: Beginner-to-intermediate strategy guide covering queen placement, blocking, ant pathing, and endgame surrounds.
take_what: the queen-placement tempo rule: the queen bee MUST be placed by a player's 4th turn at the latest, forcing every opening to resolve its central commitment within a fixed small window instead of drifting

name: Meeple Like Us - Hive (2001) design review
one_line: Accessibility-focused design critique arguing Hive's depth comes entirely from movement constraints stacked on a trivial ruleset, but at a real learnability cost.
take_what: the game separates placement rules (new pieces only touch same color, until turn 2 where they must NOT touch opponent) from movement rules (once queen is down, any legal slide/hop applies) - this placement/movement asymmetry is explicitly credited with avoiding memorized 'book openings' the way chess suffers from
constraint: note the reviewer's warning: this same depth makes new-vs-expert games un-fun, a real risk for Limen's onboarding

name: Shut Up & Sit Down - Hive Mind: How to Win at Hive Like a Master
one_line: Satirical strategy article built around real Hive board states, illustrating beetle-climb encirclement and multi-piece surround threats.
take_what: the beetle's ability to physically stack ON TOP of any piece (friend or foe), taking that hex out of play for movement purposes while itself becoming a mobile 'lid' that can be dropped onto the queen's last open hex from above - a vertical threat vector distinct from lateral siege

name: BoardGameArena forum - Mosquito, Ladybug, Pillbug expansion discussion
one_line: Player discussion of the three official Hive expansion pieces and how they interact with the base ruleset.
take_what: the Pillbug's 'toss' ability: once per turn it can grab any adjacent piece (friend or foe) and drop it into another empty hex adjacent to itself, WITHOUT that piece using its own move - but any piece moved this way (or that moved itself) is frozen and cannot move or use its ability on the opponent's very next turn, creating a forced-tempo lockout
constraint: none - mechanic idea, would need custom balancing for hex tile CCG context

name: UltraBoardGames - Additional Hive Pieces reference
one_line: Reference page detailing Mosquito ability-copying rules and Ladybug's 2-over-1-under movement.
take_what: the Ladybug's fixed movement: exactly 2 steps across the top of the hive then 1 step down to an empty hex touching the hive - a piece whose power is entirely defined by a rigid movement PATTERN rather than a stat, letting it slip behind enemy lines predictably enough to plan around but flexibly enough to surprise

name: UltraBoardGames - Tips to Win Hive
one_line: Short tips page reinforcing queen mobility and multi-threat tactics.
take_what: the 'multiple threat paths' tip: strong players deliberately create two or more simultaneous surround threats on the queen so the opponent's single defensive move can only block one, converting a numeric-advantage board state into a forced win - i.e. design for unavoidable dual-threat forks as the actual close-out mechanism, not raw material lead
